status: DESIGN APPENDIX v3 (backlog): rows for milestones M3-M5 and 'post'. Not loaded by the game and not gated by the data test; a row moves into the live file, and under test, when its milestone starts. Rows may reference live ids.
summary: Specialties, knowledge and languages, the husbandry skill and teaching modifiers.
id_rules: Ids are stable strings (prefix.name). Never rename an id once saves exist; add an alias instead. Display names are separate and may change. An id is defined in exactly one place: the live file or the backlog.

milestones.M1: A winter night: fire, shelter, cold, hunger, sleep, time safety; the fort region only; one background; 1765
milestones.M2a: A winter from the woods: living from the manor woods through the winter by your own hands (gathering, hides, sewing, snares, snowshoes, a half-faced camp, a hung cache, ice fishing); plain barter with the sutler, the trader, the garrison's soldiers, a farm family from German Flatts and an old hunter; credit and the fall outfit as options; the second background
milestones.M2b: Learning from neighbours: lessons, watching, examining, quality standards, haggling, promises and loans
milestones.M3: The year turns: the full almanac, seasons and weather content, the summer goal (bark and a cabin), fishing, frogs, ginseng, one played wage job; the fur cap and robe, leggings, carving, casting balls, the cache pit, char cloth and spruce beer
milestones.M4: People: NPC schedules and tiers at the fort, standing, invitations, the soldiers and the lieutenant as mentors; Native characters only after the relevant nation's sign-off
milestones.M5: The map: the Carry, the valley, the town and the hunting grounds, travel and camps, other markets and backgrounds
milestones.post: After M5 and not yet planned: the 1757 and 1761 starts and their eras, detailed illnesses, thirst, potash, upstream canoe and bateau travel, the Proxy NPC tier, languages beyond English, French, Mohawk and Oneida

knowledge.name: Bow-drill fire
knowledge.notes: A rare fallback by the 1750s: steel was common in trade, including in Oneida households. Learned from a backcountry hunter, a book or experiment; no fire-drill content touches ceremony without consultation.
knowledge.also: experiment: 5 failed attempts with a bow drill unlock it at a -0.1 penalty

knowledge.name: Building a bark house or hunting lodge (Haudenosaunee)
knowledge.notes: Among the Haudenosaunee men built houses and cleared land while women farmed (review 1, issue 10). Taught by the town's men, by the household's own choice; may be declined. Nation-specific names after consultation.

knowledge.name: Maple sugaring
knowledge.notes: Developed by Native peoples of the Northeast; settlers learned it. Usually taught at a working sugar camp.

knowledge.name: Parched corn meal
knowledge.notes: Called by its nation-specific name after consultation. 'Nocake' is New England Algonquian usage and is not used for Haudenosaunee towns.

knowledge.name: Winter beaver hunt at the lodge
knowledge.notes: Breaking into lodges and dams through the ice, with nets, deadfalls and guns: one real method of taking beaver [H-regional: Carlos and Lewis, N:23, describe the Hudson's Bay lowlands; not yet checked for New York]. Steel sets were also in use (N:36).

knowledge.name: Steel-trap beaver water sets
knowledge.notes: Castoreum-baited steel sets spread with cheaper traps later in the century; in the 1760s traps are scarce and dear.

knowledge.name: Worm remedies
knowledge.notes: Pinkroot is a southeastern plant taken into colonial medicine from Cherokee use in the 1750s: the surgeon and the book teach it. Local healers teach local plants, chosen with consultation (review 1 of v2, minor 12).

knowledge.name: Seneca snakeroot
knowledge.notes: Tennent's 1736 essay promoted it after Seneca use. In game it shortens chest colds; for snakebite it only steadies morale.

knowledge.name: Leaching potash
knowledge.notes: Parliament encouraged colonial potash from 1751 and the Society of Arts offered premiums; New York and New England output grew markedly from the mid-1760s, with Johnson's encouragement; the larger boom came in 1790-1820 (N:42).

knowledge.name: Weir building
knowledge.notes: Group work; the player joins a community weir before leading one.

Munsee (Delaware)

knowledge.name: Tanning with bark in a vat
knowledge.origin: A German household method: bark tanning in a vat, or tawing with alum and salt [H: verify for the valley].
